doc.title: Bela Fleck interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, December 7, 2004

chapter: Teaching, tradition and the banjo's roots
title: Advice for jazz students and what Berklee might have taught him
summary: Fleck says unusual characters succeed and creativity cannot be taught. He wishes he could read music and had learned changes, and he stresses reaching listeners and being good to play with.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Becoming a teacher: jazz in schools and conservatories

blocks.x: You’ve probably played a number of times in well known music schools, universities and so forth. Do you wonder what some of the people that are majoring in jazz now and so forth are going to do when they get out? Knowing what you do about the music business?

Yeah I think it’s tough. I mean it’s always the unusual characters that kind of do the best, the ones that don’t follow the school, that don’t follow the school of thought, that stepped outside of it in some way. And I don’t know how you teach that. I mean I know how you teach somebody, you know you can teach somebody a technical aspect of things and then they have good technique and they have good ability, but I don’t know how you teach creativity or teach somebody to write better tunes or write tunes that’ll reach out to people. I don’t know how you teach people to perform. I mean you don’t want to go to like performing school and like have somebody like Brittany Spears, like where you get on a soundstage and then your teacher critiques your mouth movements while you’re soloing, or that you don’t reach out to the audience. But I mean you could do that. But if you’re really going to teach skills that were going to help you be successful in music I would take a good hard look at how what you do reaches people. And that’s more important than whether you actually can play the right scales in the songs and to your future as a performer. But you know if you can’t play the right stuff, if you’re playing jazz and you get a gig playing with good jazz guys and you can’t cut the changes they’re not going to want to call you and that’s part of making it in show business too is working your way up to the point where you’re in front of a audience and musicians around you wanting to work with you for some reason. Or that quality of being like the kind of musician that brings out the best in other musicians. Makes people want to have you around. That’s the kind of stuff that you don’t really hear about. Those are the things that — but in terms of the technical stuff, there’s a lot of stuff I wish I knew that if I had spent three years at Berklee I would know, about getting through changes, the weird changes that come at me, or if I could read music. I don’t read music well at all. Transcribe. Maybe had a broader musical palette to draw from.
